name: Dual Decomposition
analogy: Think of it as a firm with three trading desks sharing one margin account. Instead of a central planner deciding every position, the firm posts a price per margin dollar, each desk sizes its own book given that price, and the firm raises the price when desks ask for too much and lowers it when they ask for too little.

steps.title: Split the problem into separate desks
steps.description: The model notices that the problem is made of independent pieces that are linked by only a few shared limits. Each piece, such as one strategy or one instrument, can be solved alone if it is told the price of the shared resource.
steps.inExample: Three strategies each size their own book, linked only by one shared margin account of 40,000 US dollars.

steps.title: Turn the shared limit into a price
steps.description: Instead of enforcing the shared limit directly, the model attaches a price to each unit of the shared resource and charges every desk that price. A high price discourages use, a low price encourages it.
steps.inExample: A price per 1,000 US dollars of margin is introduced, and each contract's expected edge is reduced by that price times the margin the contract uses.

steps.title: Let each desk solve its own small problem
steps.description: Given the current price, every desk independently chooses its best position size. Each extra contract earns a little less than the one before, so every desk has a natural stopping size. These small problems are easy and can run side by side.
steps.inExample: At a price of zero, the desks together ask for 81,600 US dollars of margin, far above the 40,000 available.

steps.title: Compare total demand with the shared supply
steps.description: The requests are added up and compared with what the shared resource allows. A shortage means the price is too low and an excess means it is too high.
steps.inExample: Demand of 81,600 against supply of 40,000 shows the price must rise.

steps.title: Adjust the price and ask again
steps.description: The price is moved in the direction of the shortage, by a step that shrinks over time. The desks re-solve at the new price, and the loop continues until total demand fits the supply.
steps.inExample: The price rises from zero to about 1, then just under 2, then just over 2 US dollars per 1,000 of margin, and demand falls from 81,600 to 65,100, 51,300 and finally 39,300 over 4 rounds.

steps.title: Read off the plan and the price
steps.description: At the end, each desk has a position and the shared resource is used up or nearly so. The final price is itself a result: it is the value of one more unit of the shared resource to the whole firm.
steps.inExample: The final price of about 2 US dollars per 1,000 of margin says an extra 1,000 of margin would add about 2 US dollars of expected edge.

useFor.task: Sharing one margin pool across strategies
useFor.example: Letting a trend strategy on MNQ, a mean-reversion strategy on ES and a breakout strategy on M2K size themselves independently under one account margin.
Allocating a firm-wide risk limit across instrument-level sizing rules that are each simple alone.
Working one parent order across several venues, each venue solving its own schedule given a price on the remaining size.
Distributing a capital budget across desks that each run their own optimiser, without sharing all their internal data.

avoidWhen: The pieces are strongly entangled, with many shared limits; the price loop converges slowly, so a joint solve is simpler.
Positions are whole contracts with big lumps; the demand can jump over the supply with no exact match, leaving a gap, so check the final plan against the limit.

example.scenario: Three strategies share one 40,000 US dollar margin account. Each strategy picks its own whole-contract size given a margin price, and a coordinator adjusts that price until total use fits the account. Edge figures are illustrative.

input.summary: Each strategy's edge and margin per contract, plus the shared account and a starting price.

fields.name: MNQ trend strategy
fields.value: first contract 9 US dollars edge, each next 1 less; 1,800 US dollars margin per contract
fields.meaning: Illustrative edge and margin for Micro E-mini Nasdaq-100 contracts; later contracts earn less.

fields.name: ES mean-reversion strategy
fields.value: first contract 40 US dollars edge, each next 8 less; 12,000 US dollars margin per contract
fields.meaning: Illustrative edge and margin for E-mini S&P 500 contracts; later contracts earn less.

fields.name: M2K breakout strategy
fields.value: first contract 6 US dollars edge, each next 1 less; 900 US dollars margin per contract
fields.meaning: Illustrative edge and margin for Micro E-mini Russell 2000 contracts; later contracts earn less.

fields.name: shared margin account
fields.meaning: The total margin all three strategies must fit within.

fields.name: maximum contracts per strategy
fields.meaning: The cap on contracts any one strategy may hold.

fields.name: starting price
fields.meaning: At a price of zero, each strategy asks for as much as is worth anything.

fields.name: stopping rule
fields.value: total use fits the account and is within 5 percent of it
fields.meaning: When this holds the price loop ends.

output.summary: The final price and the contracts each strategy chose at that price.

fields.name: contracts chosen
fields.meaning: The whole-number position each strategy takes at the final price.

fields.name: margin used in total
fields.meaning: 6 times 1,800 plus 2 times 12,000 plus 5 times 900, which fits the account with 700 US dollars unused.

fields.name: total expected edge
fields.meaning: 39 from MNQ plus 72 from ES plus 20 from M2K, adding up each contract's stated edge.

fields.name: final margin price
fields.value: about 2 US dollars per 1,000 of margin
fields.meaning: The value to the firm of one more 1,000 US dollars of margin.

fields.name: rounds taken
fields.meaning: The number of price adjustments before the stopping rule was met.

example.reading: The price is the useful insight: it says what extra margin is worth, so you can compare it with what your broker charges for leverage. The plan leaves 700 US dollars unused because whole contracts jump: the next ES contract needs 12,000 more. Always check the final plan against the account limit.
